questions.question: What artifacts does the verification gate read to produce its verdict?
options: Model output, system prompt, user message, tool calls
Diff, scope_report.json, rule_report.json, feedback_record.jsonl
test_results.xml, coverage.json, lint_output.txt, static_analysis.json
agent_state.json, task_board.json, AGENTS.md, requirements.txt
questions.explanation: The verification gate reads four artifact types: the diff (what changed), scope_report.json (scope check results), rule_report.json (rule compliance), and feedback_record.jsonl (what commands ran, with what exit codes).

questions.question: What is a block-severity finding and what can override it?
options: A finding that blocks the user's screen; only the agent can clear it
A finding that prevents passed: true; can only be overridden by a human with a recorded override_reason and overridden_by user id in the signed override log
A critical bug in the code that must be fixed before continuing
A finding that blocks deployment but not merging
questions.explanation: Block-severity findings prevent the gate from emitting passed: true. They can only be overridden by a human, with a signed entry in outputs/verification/overrides.jsonl containing timestamp, finding code, reason, signing user, and current HEAD commit. Agents cannot override block findings.

questions.question: Why must the verification gate be deterministic?
options: To ensure consistent performance across different hardware
Because the gate must produce the same verdict for the same artifact set every time — allowing CI to consume it reliably
To prevent any single run from having outsized influence on quality metrics
Because LLMs are non-deterministic, the gate must compensate
questions.explanation: The verification gate must be deterministic — the same artifact set always produces the same verdict. CI consumes this report; non-deterministic gates produce false alarms that erode trust. LLM judges belong in the reviewer (Lesson 39) for qualitative evaluation, not in the gate.

questions.question: What is the 'coverage floor' check and what does it prevent?
options: Checking that code coverage stays above a minimum percentage; prevents agents from deleting tests that fail to keep the gate green
Checking that all code is covered by documentation
Ensuring that all edge cases are covered by tests
A check that the scope contract covers all relevant files
questions.explanation: The coverage floor check fails the gate if measured test coverage drops below a threshold (default 80%) or below the previous merge's floor by more than 1 percentage point. Without this, agents quietly delete failing tests and the verification reports stay green while quality degrades.

questions.question: What does '--strict' mode do in a verification gate?
options: Enables additional security checks
Promotes every warning-severity finding to block severity; used for release branches and ship-blocking PRs
Runs the gate more slowly with more thorough checks
Enables all experimental gate checks
questions.explanation: --strict mode promotes every warn finding to block severity. Use for release branches, ship-blocking PRs, or post-incident triage. It is opt-in by branch — not the global default, because strict-on-everything corrodes day-to-day development flow.

questions.question: Where is the single verification report stored, and why does having one path matter?
options: In the agent's memory, accessible to all sessions
outputs/verification/<task_id>.json — one path consumed by both CI and humans prevents a fork in the source of truth
In the CI system, inaccessible to the agent
In the git history as a commit message
questions.explanation: The gate emits one outputs/verification/<task_id>.json per task. CI and humans read the same file. Multiple gates with different paths fork the source of truth — the gate report becomes ambiguous. One report, one path.
